metric.why: Liquid-cooled AI racks with coolant, manifolds, and batteries are dramatically heavier than the enterprise racks most buildings were engineered for. Retrofit projects hit structural limits before electrical ones more often than the industry expected.
metric.definition: The structural weight the raised floor or slab supports per square foot, against the actual weight of installed racks.

reading.body:
Retrofit data centers often hit structural weight limits before they run out of electrical capacity, because liquid-cooled AI racks weigh far more than the buildings were designed to support.

Most data center real estate was built for enterprise server densities. Liquid cooling systems, manifolds, and batteries on modern AI racks concentrate weight that raised floors and concrete slabs were never engineered to handle. A retrofit project can have spare power capacity at the breaker but still be unable to deploy additional servers because the floor will not support them.

This constraint is distinct from and often more restrictive than power availability. It means the binding limit on how much compute a building can hold is sometimes its structure, not its electrical supply. Expanding AI capacity in existing facilities requires either heavy structural upgrades or choosing lighter hardware, both of which delay deployment and add cost.

The data does not cover how often this occurs across the industry, how much structural reinforcement costs relative to power upgrades, or whether new-build data centers are being designed with higher load ratings as standard. It identifies the failure mode but not its prevalence.
